beats.narration_text: Ask an AI to write SQL and you get a query that looks right. The question I care about is: how would you know when it is wrong?

beats.narration_text: My final project will be CheckedSQL: a command-line tool that turns English questions into SQL for a public sample database, runs every query, and checks the result against an answer I verified by hand. It will be a GitHub repository with a test set, saved results, and a failure analysis.

beats.narration_text: I looked at asking a chat assistant directly, and Vanna.ai. They generate SQL, but they do not give me a small, reproducible record of which answers were wrong and why. CheckedSQL will. I am not claiming it is more accurate — only that its mistakes will be visible.

beats.narration_text: It will show three things from this course: a prompt contract — the model must output exactly one SELECT or a refusal; verification — every query runs on a read-only database; and evaluation — a fixed test set with saved results. The evidence will be the result files and the commit history.

beats.narration_text: What could sink it: the checker itself can be wrong. It already happened once. When I checked my own answers by hand, one of them turned out to be arbitrary: four years were tied, and my query just picked one. So every gold answer gets checked by hand, and checker mistakes are counted as their own failure category.

beats.narration_text: Why this project? It's a mix, and honestly it leans toward learning. I'm a software engineering master's student applying for SDE roles, and I wanted something a stranger can check, not something that just looks impressive. I taught myself Python and SQL basics from YouTube, but I don't have a repo that proves it yet, so this project will be that evidence. What's new to me is calling Claude from my own code, building a test set, and measuring where it fails. I chose something small on purpose, so I can finish it honestly.
